question: Does a modifiable exposure cause a disease, judged by genes that shift the exposure?

steps.title: Nature shuffles
steps.text: Each child gets a random half of each parent's variants, so the variants are not tied to lifestyle, and the disease cannot change them.

quotes.text: Genetic variation is essentially randomly inherited from parents to offspring at conception, and consequently, many factors that confound the association between the exposure and outcome cannot affect the genetic variants.
Similarly, genetic variants are generally not influenced by the outcome and therefore, by reverse causation.

steps.title: Pick variants
steps.text: Choose variants known, from large genetic studies, to shift the exposure, such as variants that raise LDL cholesterol.

quotes.text: MR studies use genetic variants robustly related to modifiable exposures to understand the influence of the exposure on various health, social, and economic outcomes.

steps.title: State assumptions
steps.text: The variants are instruments, so the instrumental variable assumptions apply: they shift the exposure, share no cause with the outcome, and reach it only through the exposure.

quotes.text: relevance (the genetic variants are associated with the exposure of interest); independence (the genetic variants share no unmeasured cause with the outcome); and exclusion restriction (the genetic variants do not affect the outcome except through their potential effect on the exposure of interest)

steps.title: Two samples
steps.text: Often the variant–exposure and variant–outcome associations come from different studies, combined from published summaries.

quotes.text: A type of MR study in which the genetic variant-exposure and genetic variant-outcome associations are estimated in different samples and combined using meta-analysis tools.

steps.title: Estimate
steps.text: Relate each variant's effect on the outcome to its effect on the exposure; the slope estimates the exposure's effect.

quotes.text: Describe the MR estimator (eg, two stage least squares, Wald ratio) and related statistics.
Secondly, some examples of natural randomisation processes can be found e.g. Mendelian randomisation, where alleles are allocated at random in offspring.

confounding.text: Concerns about violations of the independence assumption usually focus on confounding by ancestry (or population stratification).

low-power.text: If genetic variants used as instrumental variables are only weakly associated with the exposure of interest, they are said to be “weak instruments,” and then the MR estimates can be biased.
